title: Camus and the Absurd
objective: After this level you can explain Camus's absurd, the clash between our demand for meaning and a silent world, and why he pictured Sisyphus happy.
summary: For Camus the absurd is our longing for meaning meeting a silent world; he chose lucid revolt and pictured Sisyphus happy. Nagel suggested irony instead.

cards.headline: A boulder rolls back down. Forever. Could Sisyphus be happy?
cards.body: Albert Camus said yes. He meant it as an answer for everyone who has ever asked what it’s all for.

cards.headline: Not a thing but a clash
cards.body: Camus opened The Myth of Sisyphus by calling one question fundamental: whether life is worth living. His diagnosis was the absurd. It isn’t in you, and it isn’t in the world. It’s the clash between them: your “wild longing for clarity” and the “unreasonable silence of the world”. You keep asking what it’s all for, and the universe doesn’t answer.

mascot.line: Keep this: for Camus the absurd is a relationship, you asking and the world staying silent, not a fact about either one.

cards.headline: No escape hatches
cards.body: Camus refused every way out, from a leap toward hope in another life to giving up on this one. His answer was to go on living in revolt: clear-eyed, without false comfort, fully aware of life’s limits. Sisyphus, who knows his labor is hopeless and pushes on anyway, becomes the hero of the absurd.

cards.headline: Imagine him happy
cards.body: The book ends on its most famous lines: “The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.” The boulder never stays up. The pushing is the point.

cards.headline: Nagel: less drama, more irony
cards.body: Thomas Nagel doubted the heroics. In “The Absurd” (1971), he traced absurdity to our own ability to step back and see everything we take seriously as arbitrary. Defiance might make life nobler, he granted, but not less absurd. His suggested response was irony.

cards.headline: Camus and the Absurd: the big picture
learned: The absurd: our questions meet a silent world
His answer: live on, lucid, in revolt

questions.prompt: For Camus, what is the absurd?

options.label: A passing mood that only unhappy people ever have
options.rationale: For Camus it describes the human condition.

options.label: The clash between our demand for meaning and the world’s silence
The belief that nothing in the world truly exists
options.rationale: He says the world is silent, not unreal.

options.label: A simple mistake in logic that careful, patient thinking removes

questions.explanation: The absurd is the clash between our longing for clarity and meaning and the unreasonable silence of the world.

questions.prompt: Match each figure in the debate over the absurd with their key idea or image.
questions.explanation: Camus answered the absurd by living in revolt, Nagel suggested irony, and Sisyphus pushes the boulder that never stays up.

questions.prompt: Camus says we keep asking what our lives are for. Among Aristotle’s four causes, that question is looking for the _____ cause.

options.label: material
options.rationale: That asks what something is made of.

options.label: efficient
options.rationale: That asks where the change came from.

questions.explanation: The final cause is what something is for, and “what is it all for?” is exactly the question the world leaves unanswered.
